chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: I. From my grandfather Verus I learned to be gentle and mild-tempered, and to keep clear of all anger and passion. From the reputation and memory of the man who fathered me I learned both modesty and manly bearing. From my mother I learned to be religious and generous; to refrain not only from doing evil, but from even intending it; to content myself with a plain diet, and to avoid all the excesses that accompany great wealth. From my great-grandfather I learned that I should attend public schools and lecture halls, and should get good, able teachers at home; and that on such matters I ought not to begrudge excessive expense.

II. From the one who raised me I learned not to become foolishly attached to either of the two great racing factions of the circus, the Prasini and the Veneti, nor in the amphitheater to play favorites with any of the gladiators or fencers, whether the Parmularii or the Secutores. Moreover, I learned to endure hard work; to need few things; when I have a task to do, to do it myself rather than by others; not to meddle in many affairs; and not to readily entertain slander.

III. From Diognetus I learned not to busy myself with trivial things, and not easily to believe the things commonly said by those who claim to work wonders — the sorcerers, conjurers, and impostors — about the power of charms, the driving out of demons or evil spirits, and the like. I learned not to keep quails for the game, nor to be mad after such things. I learned not to be offended by other men's free speech, and to apply myself to philosophy. Him also I must thank that I first heard Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus; that I wrote dialogues in my youth; and that I took a liking to the philosopher's simple couch and the skins, and to the other things which by the Greek discipline are proper to those who profess philosophy.

IV. To Rusticus I am indebted for first entering upon the conviction that my life needed correction and cure. And then, that I did not fall into the ambition of ordinary sophists — neither to write treatises on the common theorems, nor to exhort men to virtue and the study of philosophy by public orations; and that I never, out of showmanship, tried to parade myself as an active and able man in any kind of bodily exercise. That I abandoned the study of rhetoric, poetry, and polished and elegant language. That I did not walk about the house in my long robe, nor do any such things. Moreover, I learned from him to write letters without affectation or ornament — such as the one he wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; and to be easy and ready to be reconciled and well pleased again with those who had offended me, as soon as any of them were willing to seek me out. To read with diligence; not to rest satisfied with light and superficial knowledge; not to be quick to assent to things commonly said. Him also I must thank that I ever came upon Epictetus's Hypomnemata — his moral commentaries and notes — which he gave me out of his own copy.

V. From Apollonius I learned true liberty and unshakable steadfastness, and to regard nothing at all, even in the smallest degree, but right and reason; and always, whether in the sharpest pains, or after the loss of a child, or in long illnesses, to remain the same man. He was a living and visible example to me that it was possible for the same man to be both vehement and relaxed: a man not liable to be vexed or offended at the dullness of his pupils and listeners in his lectures and expositions; and a true pattern of a man who, of all his good gifts and faculties, least esteemed in himself his excellent skill and ability to teach and persuade others in the common theorems and maxims of Stoic philosophy. From him also I learned how to receive favors and kindnesses (as they are commonly accounted) from friends, so that I might not become indebted to them on that account, nor more yielding than I ought to be, and yet not let them pass as though I were insensible and ungrateful.

VI. From Sextus I learned mildness, and the model of a household governed with paternal affection; and a purpose to live according to nature; to be grave without affectation; to carefully observe the several dispositions of my friends; not to be offended by fools, nor to attack unseasonably those who are carried away by the common opinions, with the theorems and tenets of philosophers. His conversation was an example of how a man might accommodate himself to all people and all company; so that though his company was sweeter and more pleasing than any flatterer's coaxing and fawning, yet at the same time it was most respected and revered. He also had a particular happiness and faculty in rationally and methodically finding out and setting in order all the necessary determinations and instructions for a man's life. A man without the least appearance of anger or any other passion; able at the same time most exactly to observe the Stoic Apathia — freedom from passion — and yet to be most tender-hearted; ever of good reputation, and yet almost without noise or rumor; very learned, yet making little show of it.

VII. From Alexander the Grammarian I learned to be uncensorious myself, and not reproachfully to reprove any man for a barbarism, a solecism, or a false pronunciation, but deftly, by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter — taking no notice of the word — to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.

VIII. From Fronto I learned to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannical king is subject, and how those who are commonly called εὐπατρίδαι — that is, nobly born — are in some sense incapable of, or destitute of, natural affection.

IX. From Alexander the Platonist I learned not, except in great necessity, to say or write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure,' nor in this way to keep putting off the duties we owe to our friends and acquaintances — to each in his own kind — under the pretense of urgent affairs.

X. From Catulus I learned not to despise any friend's complaint, even when unjust, but to strive to restore him to his former disposition; to speak freely and heartily well of all my teachers on any occasion, as is reported of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children with genuine affection.

XI. From my brother Severus I learned to be kind and loving to all those of my house and family. Through him also I came to know Thrasea and Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus. It was he who first put into me the idea and desire of a commonwealth of equals, administered by justice and equality; and of a kingship in which nothing should be more regarded than the good and welfare of the subjects. From him also I learned to maintain a steady course — uninterrupted by other cares and distractions — in the study and esteem of philosophy; to be bountiful and generous in the largest measure; always to hope the best; and to be confident that my friends love me. In him I further observed open dealing with those whom he reproved at any time, and that his friends could, without doubt or close observation, know what he would or would not do — so open and plain was he.

XII. From Claudius Maximus I learned in all things to strive to have command of myself, and in nothing to be carried away; to be cheerful and courageous in all sudden chances and accidents, and in sicknesses; to love mildness, and moderation, and gravity; and to do my business, whatever it might be, thoroughly and without complaining. Whatever he said, everyone believed that as he spoke, so he thought; and whatever he did, that he did it with good intent. His way was never to wonder at anything; never to be in haste, and yet never slow; nor to be perplexed, or dejected, or unseemly at any time, nor to laugh excessively; nor to be angry or suspicious, but ever ready to do good, to forgive, and to speak truth — and all this like one who seemed rather to have been born straight and right than ever to have been rectified or corrected. Nor was there any man who ever thought himself undervalued by him, or who could bring himself to think himself a better man than he was. He was also very pleasant and gracious in manner.

XIII. In my father I observed his meekness; his constancy, without wavering, in those things which after due examination and deliberation he had determined. How free from all vanity he carried himself in matters of honor and dignity, as they are esteemed; his laboriousness and persistence; his readiness to hear any man who had something to say tending to the common good; how generally and impartially he would give every man his due; his skill and knowledge of when rigor or extremity, and when remissness or moderation, was in season; how he abstained from all unchaste love of youths; his moderate accommodation to other men's affairs, as an ordinary man, neither absolutely requiring of his friends that they should wait on him at his ordinary meals, nor that they should of necessity accompany him on his journeys; and that whenever some business had to be deferred and left unfinished out of necessity, he was ever found, when he returned to it, the same man he was before. His careful examination of things in consultations, and his patient hearing of others. He would not hastily give over the investigation of a matter, as one easily satisfied with sudden notions and impressions. His care to preserve his friends: how neither at any time did he carry himself toward them with disdainful neglect and grow weary of them, nor at any time did he become madly fond of them. His contented mind in all things, his cheerful countenance, his care to foresee things far off, and to take order for the least matters without any noise or clamor. Moreover, how he suppressed all acclamations and flattery; how carefully he observed all things necessary to government, and kept an account of the common expenses, and how patiently he bore being reproached by some for this his strict and rigid dealing. How he was neither a superstitious worshiper of the gods, nor an ambitious pleaser of men, nor a pursuer of popular applause; but sober in all things, and everywhere observant of what was fitting; no affecter of novelties. In those things which conduced to his ease and convenience — of which his fortune afforded plenty — he enjoyed them without pride or bragging, yet with full freedom and liberty; so that while he freely enjoyed them without any anxiety or affectation when they were present, he found no lack of them when they were absent. Moreover, he was never commended by any man as either a learned acute man, an obsequious officious man, or a fine orator; but as a ripe and mature man, a perfectly sound man; one who could not endure to be flattered, able to govern both himself and others. Moreover, how much he honored all true philosophers, without upbraiding those who were not. His sociability, his gracious and delightful conversation, but never to the point of satiety; his care of his body within bounds and measure — not as one who desired to live long, nor as one overly studious of neatness and elegance, nor yet as one who disregarded it. So that through his own care and providence he seldom needed any inward medicine or outward application. But especially how ingenuously he would yield to any who had attained some particular faculty — eloquence, knowledge of the laws, of ancient customs, or the like; and how he concurred with them, with his best care and endeavor, that every one of them might, in his own kind, for the thing in which he excelled, be regarded and esteemed. Although he did all things carefully after the ancient customs of his forefathers, yet even of this he was not desirous that men should take notice — that he was imitating ancient customs. Again, he was not easily moved and tossed up and down, but loved to be constant both in the same places and in the same affairs; and how, after his great fits of headache, he would return fresh and vigorous to his usual affairs. Again, that secrets he had neither many nor often, and those only concerning public matters; his discretion and moderation in exhibiting public sights and shows for the pleasure and pastime of the people, in public buildings, largesses, and the like. In all these things, having regard to men only as men, and to the equity of the things themselves, and not to the glory that might follow. He never used the baths at unseasonable hours; he was no builder; he was never curious or solicitous about his food, or about the workmanship or color of his clothes, or about anything that belonged to external beauty. In all his conversation, far from all inhumanity, all boldness, and incivility, all greediness and impetuosity; never doing anything with such earnestness and intensity that a man could say of him that he sweated about it; but on the contrary, all things distinctly, as at leisure, without trouble, orderly, soundly, and agreeably. One might apply to him what is recorded of Socrates — that he knew how to want, and to enjoy, those things in the wanting of which most men show themselves weak, and in the enjoyment of which they show themselves intemperate; but to hold out firm and constant, and to keep within the compass of true moderation and sobriety in either condition, is proper to a man who has a perfect and invincible soul. Such he showed himself to be in the sickness of Maximus.

XIV. From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good domestics, loving kinsmen — almost all that I have; and that I never, through haste or rashness, transgressed against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such that such a thing (had occasion arisen) might very well have been committed by me; but that it was the mercy of the gods to prevent such a convergence of matters and occasions as might have led me to incur this blame. That I was not long brought up by the concubine of my father; that I preserved the flower of my youth; that I did not take upon me to be a man before my time, but rather put it off longer than I needed. That I lived under the government of my lord and father, who would take away from me all pride and vainglory, and bring me to the conviction that it was not impossible for a prince to live in the court without a troop of guards and followers, extraordinary apparel, certain torches and statues, and other like particulars of state and magnificence; but that a man may reduce and contract himself almost to the state of a private man, and yet not become the more base or remiss in those public matters and affairs in which power and authority are required. That I had such a brother, who by his own example could stir me up to think of myself, and by his respect and love could delight and please me. That I got ingenuous children, and that they were not born distorted or with any other natural deformity. That I was no great proficient in the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of other faculties, which perhaps I might have dwelt upon if I had found myself to succeed in them. That I promptly preferred those by whom I was brought up to such places and dignities as they seemed most to desire; and that I did not put them off with hope and expectation that — since they were still young — I would do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and Rusticus and Maximus. That I often and effectively had occasion to consider and meditate with myself concerning that life which is according to nature — what its nature and manner are; so that as for the gods and such suggestions, helps, and inspirations as might be expected from them, nothing hindered but that I might have begun long before to live according to nature; or that even now, that I was not yet partaker and in present possession of that life, I myself (in that I did not observe those inward motions and suggestions, yea, and almost plain and apparent instructions and admonitions of the gods) was the sole cause. That my body in such a life has been able to hold out so long. That I never had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea, and that afterward when I fell into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That, having been often displeased with Rusticus, I never did anything to him for which I afterward had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was to die young, yet she lived with me all her latter years. That as often as I had a purpose to help and succor any who were either poor or fallen into some present necessity, I was never answered by my officers that there was not ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never had occasion to require the like succor from any other. That I have such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of fit and able men to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children. That by dreams I have received help, as in other things, so in particular, how I might stay my casting of blood and cure my dizziness — as also that which happened to you in Cajeta, as to Chryses when he prayed by the seashore. And when I first applied myself to philosophy, that I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor spent my time either in reading the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in practicing myself in the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt upon the studies of meteors and other natural curiosities. All these things, without the assistance of the gods and of fortune, could not have been.

XV. In the country of the Quadi at Granua, these thoughts. Early in the morning say to yourself: This day I shall have to do with an idle, curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man, an unsociable, uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have come upon them through ignorance of what is truly good and truly bad. But I who understand the nature of that which is good, that it alone is to be desired, and of that which is bad, that it alone is truly odious and shameful — who know moreover that this transgressor, whoever he may be, is my kinsman, not by the same blood and seed, but by sharing in the same reason and the same divine particle — how can I either be hurt by any of these people, since it is not in their power to make me incur anything that is truly disgraceful? Or how can I be angry and ill-affected toward one who by nature is so near to me? For we are all born to be fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of the upper and lower teeth. For such parts to be in opposition is against nature; and what else is it to chafe at and be averse from, but to be in opposition?

XVI. Whatever I am is either flesh, or life-breath, or that which we commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man: reason. Away with your books! Let your mind no longer be distracted and carried to and fro; for it will not be. But, as one already on the point of death, think little of your flesh: blood, bones, and skin; a neat piece of knit and twisted work, consisting of nerves, veins, and arteries; think no more of it than so. And as for your life, consider what it is: a wind — not one constant wind either, but at every moment of an hour let out and sucked in again. The third element is your ruling part; and here consider: you are an old man; do not allow that excellent part to be brought into subjection, and to become slavish; do not allow it to be drawn up and down with unreasonable and unsociable lusts and impulses, as if with wires and sinews; do not allow it any more either to repine at anything now present, or to fear and flee anything to come, which destiny has appointed you.

XVII. Whatever proceeds from the gods directly, any man will grant, depends wholly upon their divine providence. As for those things that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even these must be conceived to depend upon nature, or upon that first and general connection and concatenation of all those things which more apparently are administered and brought to pass by the divine providence. All things flow from there; and whatever is, is both necessary and conducive to the whole (of which you are a part); and whatever is requisite and necessary for the preservation of the whole must of necessity, for every particular nature, be good and profitable. And as for the whole, it is preserved as much by the perpetual mutation and conversion of the simple elements one into another, as by the mutation and alteration of things mixed and compounded. Let these things suffice you; let them always be to you as your general rules and precepts. As for your thirst for books, away with it with all speed, that you may not die murmuring and complaining, but truly meek and well satisfied, and from your heart thankful to the gods.

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: I. Remember how long you have already put off these things, and how often, when a certain day and hour seemed to have been set for you by the gods, you neglected it. It is high time for you to understand the true nature both of the world, of which you are a part, and of that Lord and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, you yourself flowed; and that there is but a certain limit of time appointed to you, which, if you do not make use of to calm and soothe the many disorders of your soul, will pass away, and you with it, and never return.

II. Let it be your earnest and unceasing care, as a Roman and a man, to perform whatever you are about with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom, and justice; and as for all other cares and imaginations, to free your mind of them. Which you shall do if you go about every action as if it were your last — free from all vanity, from all passionate and willful deviation from reason, from all hypocrisy, self-love, and dislike of those things which by the Fates or the appointment of God have happened to you. You see that those things which are requisite and necessary for a man to keep to a prosperous course and to live a divine life are not many; for the gods will require no more of any man who keeps and observes these things.

III. Do, soul, do; abuse and despise yourself; yet a while, and the time for you to have self-respect will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends upon himself; but behold, your life is almost at an end, while, affording yourself no respect, you make your happiness consist in the souls and opinions of other men.

IV. Why should any of these things which happen externally so greatly distract you? Give yourself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro. You must also take heed of another kind of wandering: for those are idle in their actions who toil and labor in this life and have no certain goal to which to direct all their motions and desires. V. For, by not observing the state of another man's soul, scarcely was ever any man known to be unhappy. Tell anyone — whoever they may be — who do not guide by reason and discretion the motions of their own souls, that they must of necessity be unhappy.

VI. These things you must always bear in mind: what is the nature of the universe, and what is my own particular nature; what relation this has to that; what kind of part I am, and of what kind of universe; and that there is no one who can hinder you from always doing and speaking those things which are agreeable to that nature of which you are a part.

VII. Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as, after the common sense, such things I grant may be compared), says well and like a philosopher that those sins are greater which are committed through lust than those which are committed through anger. For he who is angry seems, with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn away from reason; but he who sins through lust, being overcome by pleasure, betrays in his very sin a more impotent and unmanly disposition. Well then and like a philosopher he says that of the two he is the more to be condemned who sins with pleasure than he who sins with grief. For indeed the latter may seem first to have been wronged, and so, in some manner through grief, to have been forced to be angry, whereas he who through lust commits anything did of himself simply resolve upon that action.

VIII. Whatever you plan, whatever you project, do and plan as one who, for all you know, may at this very moment depart out of this life. And as for death — if there are gods, it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do you no harm, you may be sure. But if there are no gods, or if they take no care of the world, why should I desire to live in a world empty of gods and of all divine providence? But gods there are, certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those things which are truly evil — vice and wickedness — these they have placed in a man's own power, so that he might avoid them if he would. And had there been anything besides that was truly bad and evil, they would have had a care of that also, that a man might have avoided it. But why should that be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in this world which cannot in any way make the man himself better or worse in his own person? Neither must we think that the nature of the universe either through ignorance passed over these things, or, though not ignorant of them, was unable either to prevent them or better to order and dispose them. It cannot be that she, through lack either of power or of skill, should have committed such a thing as to suffer all things, both good and bad, equally and indifferently to happen to all, both good and bad. As for life therefore, and death, honor and dishonor, labor and pleasure, riches and poverty — all these things happen to men, both good and bad, equally; but as things which of themselves are neither good nor bad, because of themselves, they are neither shameful nor praiseworthy.

IX. Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves into the matter and substance of the world; and their memories into the general age and time of the world. Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things — of those especially which either ensnare by pleasure, or are dreadful for their irksomeness, or are in great esteem and demand for their outward luster and show — how vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of all true life and being they are.

X. It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty to consider what they themselves are, in very deed, from whose bare conceits and voices honor and credit proceed; and also what it is to die — and how, if a man should consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate from it in his mind all those things which usually represent themselves to us along with it, he can conceive of it no otherwise than as a work of nature; and he who fears any work of nature is a mere child. Now death is not only a work of nature, but also conducive to nature.

XI. Consider with yourself how man, and by what part of himself, is joined to God, and how that part of man is affected when it is said to be diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul which, in a kind of circuit, compasses all things, searching (as he says) even the very depths of the earth, and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very thoughts of other men's souls, and yet is not sensible of this: that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his thoughts and cares, to the tending of that spirit which is within him, and truly and really to serve him. His service consists in this: that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, whether in regard of the gods or of men. For indeed whatever proceeds from the gods deserves respect for their worth and excellence; and whatever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be received with love, always; sometimes — as proceeding from their ignorance of what is truly good and bad (a blindness no less than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black) — with a kind of pity and compassion also.

XII. If you should live three thousand, or as many as ten thousand, years, yet remember this: that a man can part with no life properly, except that little part of life which he now lives; and that which he lives is no other than that which at every instant he parts with. That which is longest of duration, then, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although with regard to that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet the time which is now present and in being is equal to all men. And since it is this which we part with whenever we die, it manifestly appears that it can be but a moment of time that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot properly be said to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he does not have? These two things, therefore, you must remember. First, that all things in the world, from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things, ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man sees those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that the life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver, parts with, is for length and duration the very same; for only that which is present is what either of them can lose, being that only which they have; for that which he does not have, no man can truly be said to lose.

XIII. Remember that all is but opinion and conceit; for those things are plain and apparent which were spoken to Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if what is true and serious in them is received as well as what is sweet and pleasing.

XIV. A man's soul does wrong and disrespect to itself first and especially when, as much as in itself lies, it becomes an abscess and, as it were, an excrescence of the world; for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world is direct apostasy from the nature of the universe, of which all particular natures of the world are parts. Secondly, when it is either averse from any man, or led by contrary desires or affections tending to his hurt and prejudice — such as are the souls of those who are angry. Thirdly, when it is overcome by any pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when it dissembles, and covertly and falsely either does or says anything. Fifthly, when it either affects or endeavors anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due reasoning and consideration of how consequent or inconsequent it is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done without relation to the end; and the end of rational creatures is to follow and obey Him who is the reason, as it were, and the law of this great city and ancient commonwealth.

XV. The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful; in brief, as a stream are all things belonging to the body; as a dream, or as smoke, are all things that belong to the soul. Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing — philosophy. And philosophy consists in this: that a man preserve that spirit which is within him from all manner of affronts and injuries, and above all from pains and pleasures; never to do anything either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically; wholly to depend on himself and his own proper actions; to embrace contentedly all things that happen to him, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those elements of which every creature is composed. And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into another, why should that dissolution and alteration, which is so common to all, be feared by anyone? Is it not according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature can be evil. Whilst I was at Carnuntum.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: I. A man must not only consider how daily his life wastes and decreases, but also this: that if he lives long, he cannot be certain whether his understanding will continue so able and sufficient — either for discreet consideration in matters of business, or for contemplation — it being the thing on which true knowledge of things both divine and human depends. For if he should once begin to dote, his respiration, nutrition, his imaginative and appetitive and other natural faculties may still continue the same; he shall find no want of them. But how to make the right use of himself that he should, how to observe exactly in all things what is right and just, how to redress and rectify all wrong, or sudden apprehensions and imaginations, and even of this particular — whether he should live any longer or not — to consider duly; for all such things, in which the best strength and vigor of the mind are most requisite, his power and ability will be past and gone. You must hasten, therefore; not only because every day you are nearer to death than before, but also because that intellectual faculty in you, whereby you are enabled to know the true nature of things and to order all your actions by that knowledge, daily wastes and decays — or may fail you before you die.

II. This also you must observe: that whatever naturally happens to natural things has something in itself that is pleasing and delightful. A great loaf, when baked, has parts that cleave, as it were, and split apart, and make the crust of it rugged and uneven; and yet those parts of it, though in some sort it be against the art and intention of baking itself that they should thus be cleft and parted — which should have been and were first made all even and uniform — become it well nevertheless, and have a certain peculiar property to stir the appetite. So figs are accounted fairest and ripest when they begin to shrink and wither, as it were. So ripe olives, when they are next to putrefaction, are in their proper beauty. The hanging down of grapes — the brow of a lion, the froth of a foaming wild boar, and many other such things, though considered in themselves they are far from any beauty, yet because they happen naturally, they both are comely and delightful; so that if a man should, with a profound mind and apprehension, consider all things in the world, even among all those things which are but mere accessories and natural appendages as it were, there will scarcely appear anything to him in which he will not find matter of pleasure and delight. So he will behold with as much pleasure the true gape (rictus) of wild beasts as those which by skillful painters and other artificers are imitated. So he will be able to perceive the proper ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman; and whatever else it is that is beautiful and alluring in whatever exists, with chaste and continent eyes he will soon find out and discern. Those and many other things he will discern, not credible to everyone, but only to those who are truly and familiarly acquainted both with nature itself and all natural things.

III. Hippocrates, having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologers, having foretold the deaths of many, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates. Alexander and Pompey and Caius Caesar, having destroyed so many towns and cut off in the field so many thousands both of horse and foot, yet they themselves at last had to part with their own lives. Heraclitus, having written so many natural treatises concerning the last and general conflagration of the world, died afterwards all filled with water within, and all daubed with dirt and dung without. Lice killed Democritus; and Socrates, another sort of vermin — wicked, ungodly men. How, then, stands the case? You have taken ship, you have sailed, you have come to land; go out. If to another life, there also shall you find gods, who are everywhere. If all life and sense shall cease, then shall you cease also to be subject to either pains or pleasures, and to serve and tend this vile cottage — so much the viler, by how much that which ministers to it excels: the one being a rational substance and a spirit, the other nothing but earth and blood.

IV. Do not spend the remnant of your days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it you are hindered from some other better work. That is, do not spend your time in thinking what such a man does, and to what end; what he says, and what he thinks, and what he is about, and such other things or curiosities, which make a man rove and wander from the care and observation of that part of himself which is rational and overruling. See therefore, in the whole series and connection of your thoughts, that you be careful to prevent whatever is idle and irrelevant; but especially, whatever is curious and malicious. And you must accustom yourself to think only of such things that, if a man on a sudden should ask you what it is that you are now thinking, you may answer 'This' and 'That,' freely and boldly, so that by your thoughts it may immediately appear that in all of you is sincere and peaceable — as becomes one who is made for society, who regards not pleasures, nor gives way to any voluptuous imaginations at all; free from all contentiousness, envy, and suspicion, and from whatever else you would blush to confess your thoughts were set upon. He who is such is surely he who does not put off laying hold on what is best indeed, a very priest and minister of the gods, well acquainted and in good correspondence with him who is seated and placed within himself, as in a temple and sanctuary — to whom also he keeps and preserves himself unspotted by pleasure, undaunted by pain, free from any manner of wrong or insult offered by himself to himself, not capable of any evil from others; a wrestler of the best sort, and for the highest prize, that he may not be cast down by any passion or affection of his own; deeply dyed and drenched in righteousness, embracing and accepting with his whole heart whatever either happens or is allotted to him. One who, not often, nor without some great necessity tending to some public good, minds what any other either speaks, or does, or purposes; for those things only that are in his own power, or that are truly his own, are the objects of his employments, and his thoughts are ever taken up with those things which, of the whole universe, are by the Fates or Providence destined and appropriated to himself. Those things that are his own, and in his own power, he himself takes order for, that they be good; and as for those that happen to him, he believes them to be so. For that lot and portion which is assigned to every one, as it is unavoidable and necessary, so is it always profitable. He remembers besides that whatever partakes of reason is akin to him, and that to care for all men generally is agreeing to the nature of a man; but as for honor and praise, that they ought not generally to be admitted and accepted from all, but only from such as live according to nature. As for those who do not, what manner of men they are at home or abroad, day or night, how conditioned in themselves, with what manner of conditions, or with men of what conditions they toil and pass away the time together, he knows and remembers right well; he therefore regards not such praise and approbation, as proceeding from those who cannot like and approve themselves.

V. Do nothing against your will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctance. Do not affect to set out your thoughts with curious, neat language. Be neither a great talker nor a great undertaker. Moreover, let that God who is in you to rule over you find by you that He has to do with a man — an aged man, a sociable man, a Roman, a prince; one who has ordered his life, as one who expects, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all speed. One who for his word or actions needs neither an oath, nor any man to be a witness.

VI. To be cheerful, and to stand in no need either of other men's help or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity which you must be beholden to others for. Rather like one who is straight of himself, or who has ever been straight, than one who has been rectified.

VII. If you shall find anything in this mortal life better than righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better than a mind contented both with those things which according to right and reason she does, and with those which, without her will and knowledge, happen to you by providence — if, I say, you can find out anything better than this, apply yourself to it with your whole heart, and that which is best, wherever you find it, enjoy freely. But if you shall find nothing worthy to be preferred to that spirit which is within you; if nothing better than to subject to you your own lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations before you have duly considered them; nothing better than to withdraw yourself (to use Socrates's words) from all sensuality, and submit yourself to the gods, and to have care of all men in general; if you shall find that all other things, in comparison of this, are but vile and of little moment — then give not way to any other thing which, once even affected and inclined to, it will no more be in your power, without all distraction, as you ought, to prefer and to pursue after that good which is your own and your proper good. For it is not lawful that anything which is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will — whether popular applause, honor, riches, or pleasures — should be suffered to confront and contest, as it were, with that which is rational and operatively good. For all these things, if once, even for a while, they begin to please, they immediately prevail and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do you therefore, I say, absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick to it. Now, that they say is best which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand to it and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature only, reject it; and from this your tenet and conclusion, keep off carefully all plausible shows and colors of external appearance, so that you may be able to discern things rightly.

VIII. Never esteem anything as profitable which shall ever constrain you either to break your faith, or to lose your modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything that requires the secrecy of walls or veils. But he who prefers before all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of virtue which issue from it, shall never lament and exclaim, never sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company; and, which is chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus encompassed by a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even now he were to depart, he is as ready for it as for any other action which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long, this is his only care: that his mind may always be occupied with such intentions and objects as are proper to a rational, sociable creature.

IX. In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, you cannot find anything either foul or impure, or as it were festered; nothing that is either servile or affected; no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of such a one, death can never surprise as imperfect — as of an actor who should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, one might speak.

X. Use your opinative faculty with all honor and respect, for in her indeed is all: that your opinion may not beget in your understanding anything contrary to either nature or the proper constitution of a rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected toward men, and in all things willingly to submit to the gods. Casting therefore all other things aside, keep yourself to these few, and remember also that no man properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which is but a moment of time. Whatever is besides is either already past or uncertain. The time, therefore, that any man lives is but a little; and the place where he lives is but a very little corner of the earth; and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his death, even that is but little — and that too, such as it is while it is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise shall shortly die, and even while they live do not know what in very deed they themselves are, and much less can know one who long before is dead and gone.

XI. To these ever-present helps and mementos, let one more be added: ever to make a particular description and delineation, as it were, of every object that presents itself to your mind, that you may wholly and thoroughly contemplate it in its own proper nature, bare and naked; wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters; and then by yourself, in your mind, to call both it, and those things of which it consists, and into which it shall be resolved, by their own proper true names and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget true magnanimity as to be able truly and methodically to examine and consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate into their natures that at the same time this also may concur in our apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature of this universe to which it is useful? how much, in regard of the universe, may it be esteemed? how much, in regard of man, a citizen of the supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but houses and families?

XII. What is this that now my fancy is set upon? Of what things does it consist? How long can it last? Which of all the virtues is the proper virtue for this present use? — whether meekness, fortitude, truth, faith, sincerity, contentment, or any of the rest? Of everything, therefore, you must accustom yourself to say: This immediately comes from God; this, by that fatal connection and concatenation of things; or (which almost comes to one) by some coincidental casualty. And as for this, it proceeds from my neighbor, my kinsman, my fellow; through his ignorance indeed, because he does not know what is truly natural to him; but I know it, and therefore carry myself toward him according to the natural law of fellowship — that is, kindly and justly. As for those things that of themselves are altogether indifferent, as in my best judgment I conceive everything to deserve more or less, so I carry myself toward it.

XIII. If you shall attend to that which is present, following the rule of right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shall not intermix any other businesses, but shall study only this, to preserve your spirit unpolluted and pure, and shall cleave to Him without either hope or fear of anything; in all things that you shall either do or speak, contenting yourself with heroical truth, you shall live happily; and from this there is no man that can hinder you.

XIV. As physicians and surgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures, so have you always your dogmata in readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human; and whatever you do, even in the smallest things that you do, you must ever remember that mutual relation and connection that is between these two — things divine and things human. For without relation to God, you shall never speed in any worldly actions; nor, on the other side, in any divine, without some respect had to things human.

XV. Be not deceived; for you shall never live to read your moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Greeks, nor those excerpts from various books — all of which you had provided and laid up for yourself against your old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help yourself in time, if you care for yourself, as you ought to do.

XVI. To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight) — what these words mean, and in how many ways they are to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.

XVII. To be capable of fancies and imaginations is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were. To follow reason for ordinary duties and actions is common also to those who do not believe there are any gods, and who for their advantage would make no conscience of betraying their own country, and who, once the doors are shut upon them, dare do anything. If therefore all these other things are common to these likewise, it follows that the only true property of a good man is this: to like and embrace all things that happen and are destined to him; not to trouble and molest that spirit which is seated in the temple of his own breast with a multitude of vain fancies and imaginations; to keep it propitious and obey it as a god; never to speak anything contrary to truth, nor do anything contrary to justice. And such a one, though no man should believe that he lives as he does — either sincerely and conscientiously, or cheerfully and contentedly — yet is he neither with any man at all angry for it, nor diverted by it from the way that leads to the end of his life, through which a man must pass pure, ever ready to depart, and willing, of himself, without any compulsion, to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: I. That inward ruling part of man, if it is in its own true natural temper, is toward all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to accomplish, when that cannot be which at first it intended. For it never absolutely addicts and applies itself to any one object; but whatever it now intends and pursues, it pursues with exception and reservation, so that whatever falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire, when it prevails over those things that are in its way — by which things indeed a little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire soon turns them to its own nature and so consumes whatever comes in its way; yes, by those very things it is made greater and greater.
II. Let nothing be done rashly and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.

III. They seek for themselves private retreats — country villages, the seashore, mountains; yes, you yourself are apt to long much after such places. But all this, you must know, proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At whatever time you wish, it is in your power to retire into yourself, and to be at rest and free from all businesses. A man cannot anywhere retire better than to his own soul; especially he who is beforehand provided of such things within that, whenever he withdraws himself to look within, they may immediately afford him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I mean a decent, orderly disposition and bearing, free from all confusion and tumult. Afford then to yourself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew yourself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, such that as soon as you call them to mind they may suffice to purge your soul thoroughly, and to send you away well pleased with those things, whatever they be, to which now again, after this short withdrawing of your soul into herself, you return. For what is it that you are offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when you call to mind this conclusion: that all rational creatures are made one for another, that it is part of justice to bear with them, that it is against their wills that they offend; and how many already, who once likewise pursued their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out and reduced to ashes? It is time for you to make an end. As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen to you as your particular lot and portion, can you be displeased with any of them, when you call to mind that our ordinary dilemma — either a providence, or Democritus's atoms — and with it, whatever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for your body, what can you fear, if you consider that your mind and understanding, when once it has collected itself and knows its own power, has no interest at all in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or harshly and rudely), but is altogether indifferent; and whatever else you have heard and assented to concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of your honor and reputation will perhaps distract you? How can that be, if you look back and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after, all things; and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variability of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place in which it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they who will commend you? What remains, then, but that you often put in practice this kind of retiring of yourself to this little part of yourself; and above all things, keep yourself from distraction, and intend nothing vehemently, but be free and consider all things as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things which to consider and look into you must practice withdrawing yourself, let these two be among the most obvious and ready at hand: one, that the things or objects themselves do not reach to the soul, but stand without, still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within that all the tumult and all the trouble proceed. The next, that all these things which now you see shall within a very little while be changed and be no more; and ever call to mind how many changes and alterations in the world you yourself have already been an eyewitness of in your time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.

IV. If to understand and to be reasonable is common to all men, then is that reason, for which we are called reasonable, common to all. If reason is general, then is that reason also which prescribes what is to be done and what not, common to all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonwealth. If so, then the world is, as it were, a city. For of what other commonwealth can all men be said to be members? From this common city it is that understanding, reason, and law are derived to us; for from where else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist is imparted from some other element; as my breath and life has its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me — for there is nothing which does not proceed from something, as also there is nothing that can be reduced to mere nothing — so also is there some common beginning from which my understanding has proceeded.

V. As generation is, so also is death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again; a thing surely that no man ought to be ashamed of, since it is in a series of other fatal events and consequences to which a rational creature is subject — not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.

VI. Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He who would not have such things happen is like one who would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this: that within a very little while, both you and he shall both be dead; and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall remain.

VII. Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then there is no more any such thing as wrong. That which does not make the man himself worse cannot make his life worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.

VIII. Whatever happens in the world happens justly, and if you take good heed, you shall find it so. I do not mean only in right order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice, and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as you have begun; and whatever you do, do it not without this proviso: that it be a thing of that nature which a good man (as the word good is properly taken) may do. This observe carefully in every action.
IX. Do not conceive such things as he who wrongs you conceives, or would have you conceive; but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.

X. These two rules you must always have in readiness. First, do nothing at all but what reason, proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall, for the good and benefit of men, suggest to you. And secondly, if any man who is present shall be able to rectify you, or to turn you from some erroneous persuasion, that you be always ready to change your mind; and this change should proceed, not from any respect of any pleasure or credit depending thereon, but always from some probable apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be furthered, or from some other such inducement.
XI. Have you reason? I have. Why then do you not make use of it? For if your reason does her part, what more can you require?

XII. As a part, until now you have had a particular subsistence; and now shall you vanish away into the common substance of Him who first begot you, or rather, you shall be taken up again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar; one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.

XIII. Within ten days, if it so happens, you shall be esteemed a god by those who now, if you shall return to the dogmata and to the honoring of reason, will esteem you no better than a mere brute, or an ape.
XIV. Not as though you had thousands of years to live. Death hangs over you; while yet you live, while you may, be good.

XV. How much time and leisure does he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbor has said, or has done, or has attempted, but only what he does himself, that it may be just and holy! — or, to express it in Agathon's words, not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run straight on in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.

XVI. He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death does not consider that they themselves by whom he is remembered shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise who succeed them; until at last all memory, which until now by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying has had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they who shall remember you, and your memory with them, should be immortal — what is that to you? I will not say to you after you are dead, but even to you living, what is your praise? — except for some secret and politic consideration, which we call oikonomian, or dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of nature whatever is commended in you, what might be objected from that — let that now, since we are upon another consideration, be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatever it be, and in whatever respect it is fair and goodly, is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member; that therefore which is praised is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things commonly called fair and good, such as are commended either for the matter itself or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth, or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those either becomes good or fair because commended, or, being disparaged, suffers any damage? Does the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile, if it is not commended? Does gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that does, though never so common — a knife, a flower, or a tree?

XVII. If it is so that souls remain after death (say those who will not believe it), how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to contain the bodies of those who are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatever it be) makes place for other dead bodies, so the souls after death, transferred into the air, after they have sojourned there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational substance from which all others proceed, and so give way to those souls who, before coupled and associated with bodies, now begin to subsist single. This, on a supposition that the souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And here, besides the number of bodies so buried and contained by the earth, we may further consider the number of various beasts eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of truth? — to divide things into that which is passive and material, and that which is active and formal.

XVIII. Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just; and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy that presents itself.

XIX. Whatever is expedient to you, O World, is expedient to me; nothing can either be unseasonable to me, or out of date, which to you is seasonable. Whatever your seasons bear shall ever by me be esteemed as happy fruit and increase. O Nature! from you are all things, in you all things subsist, and to you all tend. Could he say of Athens, 'You lovely city of Cecrops'; and shall not you say of the world, 'You lovely city of God'?

XX. They commonly say: Do not meddle with many things, if you wish to live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions — to such and so many only as reason, in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will procure not only that cheerfulness which proceeds from the goodness, but also that which proceeds from the paucity of actions. For since it is so that most of those things we either speak or do are unnecessary, if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure and save much trouble; and therefore at every action a man must privately, by way of admonition, suggest to himself, 'What? may not this that I am now going about be of the number of unnecessary actions?' Neither must he accustom himself to cut off actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also that are unnecessary; for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.

XXI. Try also how a good man's life — of one who is well pleased with those things, whatever they be, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and who can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future — will agree with you. You have had experience of that other kind of life; make now trial of this also. Trouble yourself no more henceforth; reduce yourself to perfect simplicity. Does any man offend? It is against himself that he offends; why should it trouble you? Has anything happened to you? It is well; whatever it be, it is that which, of all the common chances of the world, from the very beginning, in the series of all other things that have or shall happen, was destined and appointed to you. To comprehend all in a few words: our life is short; we must endeavor to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.

XXII. Either this world is a kosmos, or comely piece, because all is disposed and governed by a certain order; or, if it be a mixture, though confused, yet is it still a comely piece. For is it possible that in you there should be any beauty at all, and yet that in the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? — and all things in it, too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and distinguished, and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy, one to another united, as they are?

XXIII. A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; a hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurrilous, a fraudulent, a tyrannical — what then? If he is a stranger in the world who does not know the things that are in it, why not also be a stranger who wonders at the things that are done in it?

XXIV. He is a true fugitive who flees from reason, by which men are sociable. He is blind who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding. He is poor who stands in need of another, and does not have in himself all things needful for this life. He is an abscess on the world who, by being discontented with those things that happen to him in the world, as it were apostatizes and separates himself from common nature's rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this to you, whatever it be, that first brought you into the world. He raises sedition in the city who, by irrational actions, withdraws his own soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.

XXV. There is one who, without so much as a coat, and another who, without so much as a book, puts philosophy in practice. 'I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I do not depart from reason,' says one. But I say: 'I want the food of good teaching and instructions, and yet I do not depart from reason.'

XXVI. Whatever art and profession you have learned, endeavor to affect it and comfort yourself in it; and pass the remainder of your life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatever belongs to him to the gods; and as for men, carry yourself neither tyrannically nor servilely toward any.

XXVII. Consider in your mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian; you shall see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that age quite over and ended? Again, consider now the times of Trajan. There likewise you see the very same things, and that age also is now over and ended. In like manner consider other periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after they had with all their might and main intended and pursued some one worldly thing or other, did soon after drop away, and were resolved into the elements. But especially you must call to mind those whom you yourself in your lifetime have known much distracted about vain things, and meanwhile neglecting to do that, and closely and inseparably (as fully satisfied with it) to adhere to it, which their own proper constitution did require. And here you must remember that your bearing in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of it; for so shall you not easily be tired out and vexed, if you shall not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.

XXVIII. Those words which once were common and ordinary are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Caeso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian, then Antoninus Pius — all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world, as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them who once shined as the wonders of their ages; for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? All is vanity. What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? Only this: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful; that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatever shall happen to us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning and such a fountain, from which both you yourself and all things are. Willingly, therefore, and wholly surrender yourself to that fatal concatenation, yielding yourself up to the Fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.

XXIX. Whatever is now present, and from day to day has its existence — all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves — incessantly consider: all things that are, have their being by change and alteration. Accustom yourself therefore often to meditate upon this: that the nature of the universe delights in nothing more than in altering those things that are, and in making others like to them. So that we may say that whatever is, is but as it were the seed of that which shall be. For if you think that that only is seed which either the earth or the womb receives, you are very simple.

XXX. You are now ready to die, and yet you have not attained to that perfect simplicity; you are yet subject to many troubles and perturbations, not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed toward all men as you should be, or so affected as one whose only study and only wisdom is to be just in all his actions.
XXXI. Behold and observe what is the state of their rational part; and those whom the world accounts wise — see what things they flee and are afraid of, and what things they hunt after.

XXXII. In another man's mind and understanding your evil cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of your body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of your soul. Wherein, then, but in that part of you, can the conceit and apprehension of any misery subsist? Let not that part, therefore, admit any such conceit, and then all is well. Though your body, which is so near it, should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction, yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these be still at rest; that is, let her judge this: that whatever it is that may equally happen to a wicked man and to a good man is neither good nor evil. For that which happens equally to him who lives according to nature and to him who does not, is neither according to nature nor against it; and consequently, neither good nor bad.

XXXIII. Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul; and how all things in the world are terminated into one sensitive power, and are done by one general motion, as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen.
XXXIV. What are you, that better and divine part excepted, but, as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?

XXXV. To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything has appeared and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently be out of sight.

XXXVI. Whatever happens in the world is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of the same nature are sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and whatever else ordinarily to fools is the occasion of either joy or sorrow. That which comes after, whatever it is, always very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follows upon that which was before. For you must consider the things of the world not as a loose independent number, consisting merely of necessary events, but as a discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There is then to be seen in the things of the world not a bare succession, but an admirable correspondence and affinity.

XXXVII. Let that saying of Heraclitus never be out of your mind: that the death of earth is water, and the death of water, air; and the death of air, fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was ignorant of where the way did lead, and how that reason, being the thing by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are continually and most inwardly conversant with, yet is the thing with which they are ordinarily most in opposition; and how those things which daily happen among them cease not daily to be strange to them; and that we should not either speak or do anything as men in their sleep, by opinion and bare imagination — for then we think we speak and do; and that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example for best reason, alleging their bare kathoti pareilēphamen, 'as by successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.'

XXXVIII. Even as if any of the gods should tell you, 'You shall certainly die tomorrow, or the next day,' you would not, unless you were extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit to die the next day after rather than tomorrow (for, alas, what is the difference!); so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die many years later rather than the very next day.

XXXIX. Let it be your perpetual meditation how many physicians, who once looked so grim and so theatrically knit their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after with great ostentation they had foretold the death of others; how many philosophers, after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolence abused their power upon men's lives, as though they themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns — Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable — are dead and gone. Run over also those whom you yourself, one after another, have known in your time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another; and all things in a short time. For herein lies all indeed: ever to look upon all worldly things as things for their continuance that are but for a day, and for their worth, most vile and contemptible. As for example: What is man? That which but the other day, when he was conceived, was vile slime, and within a few days shall be either an embalmed carcass or mere ashes. Thus must you, according to truth and nature, thoroughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented — even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bore her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.
XL. You must be like a promontory of the sea, against which, though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it those swelling waves are stilled and quieted.

XLI. 'Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance has happened!' Nay, happy I, to whom, this thing having happened, I can continue without grief — neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened to any man; but any man, having such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why then should that rather be an unhappiness than this a happiness? But however, can you, O man, term that unhappiness which is no mischance to the nature of man? Can you think that a mischance to the nature of man which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What then have you learned is the will of man's nature? Does that then which has happened to you hinder you from being just? or magnanimous? or temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? — or from anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession of which the nature of man (as then enjoying all that is proper to her) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude: upon all occasion of sorrow, remember henceforth to make use of this dogma — that whatever has happened to you is in very deed no such thing of itself as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously is certainly great happiness.

XLII. It is but an ordinary, coarse one, yet it is a good and effectual remedy against the fear of death for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such as greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more than those whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime, having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life is but little; and, as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore to you altogether as a matter of indifference. For if you shall look backward, behold, what an infinite chaos of time presents itself to you; and as infinite a chaos, if you shall look forward.
